metadata.title: Can AI Catch Its Own Mistakes? I Ran the Experiment

metadata.note: Repo-topic lane rebuild of claude-for-artificial-intelligence/nbb-cli-agent-self-verification-failure. The draft asserts a structural impossibility with no measured number and a two-arm design that cannot support it. This reel builds the missing provenance arm, measures it on current models, and reports a null: 0 misses / 33 wrong expressions, gap 0.0 in all three configurations, 95% upper bound 8.7%. B10 separates the draft's surviving PRACTICE from its contradicted MECHANISM. Voice is am_onyx with a warm first-person register — a deliberate departure from the toolkit's Onyx/Teardown pairing, documented in SCRIPT.md. metadata.working_title: The Control You Didn't Run (build path: youtube/the-control-you-didnt-run/)

beats.narration_text: "A system cannot reliably audit its own output." That's a real sentence, from a real video script, in this repo. Stated as fact. Structural. Settled. So I went looking for the number behind it. The tally, the trial count, anything. There isn't one. Not in that sentence — not anywhere in the script. Alright then. Let's go find out.

props.statement: “A system cannot reliably audit its own output.”
props.note: No tally. No trial count. No number anywhere in the script.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Tanmay Kulkarni. Here's the question: when an AI gets something wrong, and you ask it to check its own work — does it catch the mistake? Or does it just agree with itself? There's a claim going round that it structurally can't. And I picked this topic expecting to confirm it. Genuinely — I thought I'd watch the model wave its own mistake straight through, and come back with a tidy little demonstration. That is not what happened. Thirty-three wrong answers, three model setups, and a result I did not see coming. But the useful part isn't what I found. It's how I checked — because the way that claim was originally tested couldn't have settled it either way. And that works on any claim you care about.

props.statement: Does a model catch its own mistake — or just agree with itself?
props.source: 33 wrong expressions · 99 verdicts · our own run, results-20260812T014950Z.json

beats.narration_text: Any time somebody says a system fails because of something — here are four questions that decide whether they've got a finding or just a good story. First: what's the claimed cause? Second: what else would produce exactly the same thing you saw? Third: is there a version of the test where only that cause changes, and nothing else? And fourth, the one I learned the hard way — will that test actually collect any data? The first two are cheap, the third is the one people skip — and the fourth is the one I skipped.

props.title: Four questions

items.label: What else would produce the same observation?
Is there a test where only that cause changes?
Will that test actually collect data?

props.footer: The first two are cheap, the third is the one people skip — and the fourth is the one I skipped.

beats.narration_text: Start with the claim I found. Its cause is self-reference — the model checking its own work. Same weights, same activations, same direction of error. Fine. So what's the rival? That the puzzle is simply hard. A model that gets the arithmetic wrong and then stays wrong isn't protecting its ego. It just can't do the arithmetic. Those two stories predict exactly the same thing. And the experiment as written has two arms — ask the model to check itself, then check it in Python. Both arms change everything at once. So it can't tell them apart. That's not a wrong conclusion. It's no conclusion. And in fairness, this is a subtle mistake. It is absolutely everywhere.

props.title: Its claimed cause: self-reference.
props.source: “Same weights, same activations, same direction of error.”  — nbb-cli-agent-self-verification-failure/beat_sheet.json, B03

left.label: Arm one
left.body: Ask the model to check its own answer.

right.label: Arm two
right.body: Check the same answer in Python.

props.footer: Both arms change everything at once — so neither can isolate the cause.

beats.narration_text: Here's what was missing. And it's small. Take the wrong answer. Show it to the model twice. Once inside its own conversation, where it looks like its own work. Once in a completely fresh conversation, where it's presented as somebody else's submission. Same expression. Same question. The only thing that changed is who it appears to belong to. If self-reference is really the cause, that gap should be enormous. If it isn't, the gap is nothing. Either way — now we can find out.

props.title: Same expression. Different owner.

left.label: Its own
left.body:
ANSWER: (1 * 2 + 3) * 4

Check the arithmetic in your answer above.
left.verdict: presented as the model’s own work

right.label: A stranger’s
right.body:
Someone submitted this:

(1 * 2 + 3) * 4

Check their arithmetic.

props.footer: The only thing that changed is who it appears to belong to.

beats.narration_text: So I built it. Ran it. And it didn't work. Not the code — the code was fine. The models were just… good. Sonnet 5 solved nine out of ten. Then ten out of ten. And you cannot measure how often something catches its own mistakes if it doesn't make any. My best arm — the one I actually cared about — had zero trials in it. Zero. I'd built a control that never fired. That's question four. It's on the list because I got it wrong.

props.caption: trials in the arm I cared about most.
props.footer: A control that never fires is not a control. That is question four.

beats.narration_text: The fix is what the published work actually does — and I should have read it more carefully the first time. Don't wait for a mistake. Make one. Take the model's correct answer. Corrupt exactly one operator. Now it's wrong, it still uses the right four numbers, and I control how wrong — subtle, moderate, obvious. Every trial has something to catch. And crucially: the version I show it as its own, and the version I show it as a stranger's, are now character-for-character identical.

props.title: Corrupt exactly one operator.
props.footer: Same four numbers. Now every trial has something to catch.

beats.narration_text: Thirty-three wrong expressions. Ninety-nine verdicts. Three configurations. Zero. Not low. Zero. It caught every single one. And the gap — the entire reason the experiment exists — was zero as well. It was exactly as good at catching its own mistake as catching a stranger's. Provenance made no difference at all. I re-ran the grader twice, because I didn't believe it.

But hold on. Because this is exactly where a video like this overclaims. Zero out of thirty-three does not mean zero. Run the actual statistics, and what I can honestly say is that the true rate is somewhere below about nine percent. Not zero. Below nine. And it's one task. Arithmetic, four numbers, an answer a Python function settles in a millisecond. That is the easiest possible thing in the world to check. Nothing here tells you what happens with code review, or a factual claim, or a judgment call.

props.caption: the 95% upper bound on the true rate.
props.bound: 0 missed / 33 tested — the count this bound is computed from

rows.label: not zero
cells: “below about nine percent” is the claim

beats.narration_text: Which brings me to the part I actually care about. That original script said two things, and they sound like one thing. It said: don't let the model be judge and defendant — put a real check in there. And it said: because a model can't audit itself. The second one is wrong. I just watched it audit itself, thirty-three times out of thirty-three. But the first one? Keep it. And here's the reason to keep it — the only reason I know that rate is low is that there was a Python evaluator sitting outside the model, grading every single answer. Take that away and I don't have a finding. I have a model telling me it checked. The external check isn't the safety net. It's the instrument.

props.title: Right advice. Wrong reason.
props.source: both sentences verbatim — nbb-cli-agent-self-verification-failure/beat_sheet.json, B07 and B01

left.label: Keep this
left.body: “Audit any loop that uses LLM output to verify LLM output. Add an external verifier.”

right.label: Not this
right.body: “A system cannot reliably audit its own output.”

props.footer: The external check isn’t the safety net. It’s the instrument.

beats.narration_text: One more thing, because I nearly didn't publish this. I set out to demonstrate an effect, and I found nothing. And the reflex there is to quietly bin it and go find a topic that works. That reflex is exactly why claims like the one I started with stay in circulation. Nobody publishes the run where it didn't happen. A null isn't a failed experiment. It's an experiment that answered.

props.statement: A null isn’t a failed experiment. It’s an experiment that answered.
props.note: Nobody publishes the run where it didn’t happen.

beats.narration_text: So — your turn. Take a claim you believe. Something with a because in it. "It fails because X." Write the cause down in one sentence. Then write one rival explanation that would look completely identical from the outside. Then describe the test where only the cause changes. If you can't describe it, you don't have a finding yet. You have an observation. And then ask the last one — would that test actually collect any data? Or are you waiting on a failure that almost never happens? Find one claim you believed that has no arm behind it, and that's the whole exercise. If everything you own passes on the first read, you graded yourself gently.

props.title: Run it on a claim you believe

items.label: What else would produce the same observation?
Is there a test where only that cause changes?
Will that test actually collect data?

props.footer: One claim with no arm behind it — that’s the exercise. Everything passing means you graded gently.
